documents.text: Investment Opportunities in Artificial Intelligence (AI) Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the global economy through advances in generative AI, cloud computing, semiconductor design, cybersecurity, robotics, and enterprise software integration. We have all heard the expression, “The cobbler’s 'children have no shoes.” It could likely be said ITIS Professors have no “Technology stock portfolios!” This paper examines stock market opportunities across key companies positioned to benefit from accelerating AI adoption in both consumer and enterprise markets. We examine firms that control critical infrastructure layers of the AI ecosystem, including chip manufacturing, hyperscale cloud platforms, data management, and software applications. Special attention is given to those firms that could possibly be the next big “Killer App” and produce exponential returns on investments! Among semiconductor leaders, NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) has emerged as the dominant supplier of graphics processing units (GPUs) used in machine learning and large language models. Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE: TSM) represent additional growth opportunities through advanced chip fabrication and accelerator competition. In cloud computing, Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZ), and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) continue investing heavily in AI-enabled platforms and enterprise productivity solutions. Enterprise software firms such as Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) and Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) are leveraging AI-driven analytics and automation to improve operational efficiency and customer engagement. The TREO also evaluates investment risks, including regulatory uncertainty, valuation volatility, supply chain dependencies, and increasing global competition. Although many AI-related equities trade at historically elevated valuation multiples, long-term demand for computational infrastructure and intelligent automation suggests sustained growth potential. For business and information technology scholars, the AI sector provides a valuable case study in technological disruption, strategic innovation, and capital market behavior. The author suggests that diversified exposure across semiconductors, cloud infrastructure, and enterprise software may provide the most balanced approach for private investors seeking participation in the expanding AI economy. We are hopeful this TREO will generate some lively discussions.

Artificial intelligence applications in medicinal and aromatic plants: a review of cultivation, phytochemical profiling, drug discovery, and processing energy Medicinal and aromatic plants are vital for global healthcare and drug discovery, but their sustainable use is challenged by inefficient cultivation, inconsistent quality, and energy‑intensive processing. Artificial intelligence offers powerful tools to address these problems. This review provides a comprehensive and accessible synthesis of AI applications across the entire value chain of these plants. Major application domains include cultivation, where AI assists in species identification, disease diagnosis, and optimization of water, nutrient, and energy inputs; phytochemical profiling, where machine learning models predict bioactive compound concentrations, authenticate geographical origins, and optimize extraction protocols; drug discovery, where AI enables virtual screening of phytochemicals, network pharmacology, and decoding of synergistic effects in herbal formulations; and processing energy, where AI is applied to reduce energy consumption in drying, distillation, and solvent extraction, with quantitative data on energy intensities and savings. The review also covers AI integration with traditional knowledge and in vitro biotechnology. Performance claims are critically evaluated, including dataset sizes, validation methods, and real‑world applicability. Key challenges such as data scarcity, model interpretability, and ethical concerns are discussed, and a future roadmap is outlined. By synthesizing the current state of AI in medicinal and aromatic plant research, this review serves as a practical resource for researchers, farmers, and industry professionals seeking to harness AI for more sustainable and efficient production of high‑value botanical products.

Nanophotonic Semiconductors and Advanced Materials Intelligence for Sustainable Computing and DeepTech Innovation Abstract: Nanophotonic semiconductors and advanced materials intelligence are emerging as a unified foundation for energy-efficient computation, optical communication, precision sensing, quantum and neuromorphic systems, and resilient industrial innovation. This monograph develops a multiscale scholarly architecture linking material composition, electronic structure, nanoscale geometry, light-matter interaction, fabrication processes, device performance, system integration and lifecycle sustainability. It advances research designs that treat uncertainty, reproducibility and governance as integral parts of scientific reasoning. Statistical chapters formulate hierarchical, causal, Bayesian and reliability models for explaining process-structure-property relationships and supporting robust multiobjective decisions. Machine-learning chapters examine multimodal representation learning, physics-informed operators, generative inverse design, transfer across laboratories and foundries, and assurance through calibration, interpretability and monitoring. A scalable engineering lifecycle connects semantic data architectures, digital twins, high-performance and edge computing, provenance, MLOps and cybersecurity. Sectoral analysis extends the framework to optical interconnects, sustainable accelerators, environmental and health sensing, quantum and secure communication, circular manufacturing and regional innovation systems. Throughout, the analysis connects South Asian, European, African and American research ecosystems while emphasizing evidence quality, material responsibility, supply resilience and public value. The resulting models, protocols, metrics and governance artifacts support adaptation into research handbooks, advanced curricula, industrial roadmaps and multi-year DeepTech programmes. Keywords nanophotonics, semiconductor materials, advanced materials intelligence, sustainable computing, light-matter interaction, photonic integrated circuits, inverse design, materials informatics, physics-informed machine learning, neural operators, causal inference, Bayesian calibration, reliability engineering, digital twins, scientific MLOps, optical interconnects, neuromorphic photonics, quantum photonics, lifecycle assessment, circular electronics, semiconductor manufacturing, trustworthy artificial intelligence, DeepTech governance, planetary resilience

Side-Mounted Rolling Contact Interconnect for Planar Stackable Semiconductor Packages This paper proposes a conceptual semiconductor packaging architecture inwhich electrical interconnections are relocated from the bottom surface to themiddle region of the package sidewalls. Instead of conventional solder balls orbottom-pad arrays, the concept employs miniature rolling conductive contactspositioned around the package perimeter.The objective is to investigate whether such an architecture could improvemechanical compliance, modularity, serviceability, and package density forfuture AI accelerators, memory modules, storage devices, and heterogeneouschiplet systems.

A Sustainable 3D IC Packaging Solution with Integrated Microfluidic Cooling and Thermoelectric Energy Recycling The semiconductor industry has long depended on shrinking transistor dimensions to improve performance. However, as technology approaches the 2 nm node, traditional 2D scaling is reaching fundamental physical and manufacturing limits. As a result, the industry is rapidly transitioning toward 3D IC architectures as the next viable pathway for continued system-level improvement. To meet the growing computational demands of AI accelerators and high-performance computing (HPC), advanced 2.5D and 3D packaging technologies such as TSMC’s CoWoS®, InFO®, and SoIC® have become key approaches for delivering high-bandwidth chiplet connectivity and extremely dense vertical stacking. Despite these advancements, current 3D IC solutions remain constrained by TSV- and RDL-based structures. TSV fabrication involves deep reactive-ion etching, dielectric lining, seed layer deposition, and high-aspect-ratio copper filling, all of which increase cost, process complexity, and yield risk. RDL networks also encounter signal attenuation, crosstalk, and impedance interference, especially at GHz frequencies. More critically, the co-packaging of high-power logic dies with vertically stacked high-bandwidth memory (HBM) results in extreme thermal congestion, as large amounts of heat generated by the logic processor must dissipate through a confined vertical structure with limited heat-spreading paths. This thermal bottleneck leads to elevated junction temperatures, and the formation of localized hotspots that reduce reliability. As power densities continue to rise in AI and HPC chips, these thermal and interconnect challenges increasingly threaten to limit the practical scalability of existing 3D IC architectures. Therefore, in this study, we develop an innovative 3D IC packaging platform that simultaneously addresses both structural and thermal limitations that currently restrict the scalability and performance of advanced heterogeneous systems. This platform employs a modular fabrication strategy that supports unlimited vertical stacking, enabling highly flexible system architecture design, and incorporates ultra-high-aspect-ratio metal vias to achieve dense, low-resistance, and highly reliable vertical interconnection. Beyond the structural innovation, the platform integrates two complementary thermal management mechanisms: embedded microfluidic cooling channels and thermoelectric thin-film layers. The microfluidic channels provide active and localized heat removal, reducing the chip temperature from 70.3 °C to 49.7 °C, as demonstrated in Figure 1(A). Meanwhile, the thermoelectric layer enables direct waste-heat harvesting, converting temperature gradients into usable electrical energy. As a result, the thermoelectric voltage output increases from 0.15 mV to 0.52 mV, as shown in Figure 1(B), reflecting a substantial improvement in waste-heat utilization. Collectively, these innovations introduce a fundamentally new direction for 3D IC architectures, establishing a thermally aware, energy-recycling, and environmentally sustainable platform capable of redefining future developments in 3D heterogeneous integration. Artificial Intelligence, Internet of Things, and Advanced Semiconductor Technologies for Intelligent Edge Computing Systems: Challenges, Opportunities, and Future Directions The rapid expansion of Internet of Things (IoT) devices and the growing demand for real-time intelligent services have accelerated the adoption of edge computing as a fundamental computing paradigm. The convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), IoT, and advanced semiconductor technologies has enabled the development of intelligent edge computing systems capable of processing large volumes of data with low latency, reduced energy consumption, and enhanced security. Recent advances in semiconductor technologies, including FinFETs, Gate-All-Around Field-Effect Transistors (GAAFETs), System-on-Chip (SoC) platforms, AI accelerators, neuromorphic processors, and RISC-V architectures, have significantly improved the computational capabilities and energy efficiency of edge devices. At the same time, AI techniques such as deep learning, TinyML, federated learning, and reinforcement learning have enabled intelligent data analytics, autonomous decision-making, and privacy-preserving inference directly on resource-constrained edge devices. This paper investigates the integration of AI, IoT, and advanced semiconductor technologies for developing intelligent edge computing systems. It presents a unified architecture that illustrates the interaction between semiconductor hardware, IoT communication networks, edge computing platforms, and AI-driven analytics to support real-time applications. The study analyzes the impact of emerging semiconductor technologies on edge intelligence and evaluates their role in improving computational performance, energy efficiency, scalability, and system reliability. In addition, the paper discusses the application of intelligent edge computing in smart healthcare, Industry 5.0, smart cities, intelligent transportation, precision agriculture, and environmental monitoring. Key technical challenges, including resource limitations, interoperability, cybersecurity, privacy preservation, thermal management, and sustainable hardware design, are critically examined. Finally, future research opportunities involving heterogeneous chiplet architectures, neuromorphic computing, quantum-inspired AI accelerators, 6G-enabled AIoT, and green semiconductor manufacturing are identified. The proposed perspective provides a comprehensive foundation for designing next-generation intelligent edge computing systems capable of supporting emerging digital ecosystems.

From Market Signal to Policy Signal: Samsung Electronics, HBM Competition, and South Korea's Semiconductor Resilience This policy brief argues that Samsung Electronics' current market valuation should be interpreted not merely as a corporate finance phenomenon but as a forward-looking indicator of South Korea's semiconductor competitiveness and industrial resilience. Rather than estimating intrinsic value through a conventional discounted cash flow (DCF) approach, the analysis employs a reverse discounted cash flow (reverse DCF) methodology that infers the long-run profitability assumptions embedded in Samsung's prevailing share price. By progressively tightening assumptions regarding revenue growth, capital expenditure intensity, discount rates, explicit-period margins, and available cash balances across five increasingly conservative model specifications, the analysis estimates that equity markets are implicitly pricing Samsung's terminal EBIT margin at approximately 2.5–4.4%, a profitability range historically associated with commoditised manufacturing rather than technological leadership. This contrasts sharply with Samsung's historical semiconductor margins exceeding 12% over the past decade and reaching approximately 18% during cyclical peaks, suggesting that markets are pricing the possibility of structural erosion rather than temporary earnings weakness. The paper reframes this market-implied valuation as a diagnostic tool for industrial policy, arguing that Samsung's position as South Korea's largest memory semiconductor producer, major exporter, taxpayer, and vertically integrated technology firm makes its valuation indicative of broader national industrial capability rather than isolated firm performance. The brief identifies four interconnected structural vulnerabilities underpinning the market discount. First, Samsung has ceded leadership in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to SK Hynix, which secured first-mover advantage in HBM3E production and NVIDIA qualification, allowing it to dominate the AI memory market through manufacturing learning effects, customer relationships, and cost advantages. Second, Samsung Foundry continues to experience structural operating losses due to persistent deficits in manufacturing yield, ecosystem maturity, and technology competitiveness relative to TSMC, limiting South Korea's participation in advanced logic manufacturing. Third, exceptionally high capital expenditure requirements—averaging 14–19% of annual revenue—reduce free cash flow available for strategic reinvestment, innovation, and technological adaptation as semiconductor manufacturing becomes increasingly capital intensive. Fourth, geopolitical pressures simultaneously constrain Samsung's Chinese manufacturing operations through tightening U.S. export controls while exposing commodity memory businesses to increasing competition from emerging Chinese semiconductor firms, creating a strategic "pincer effect" that narrows Samsung's technological and capital allocation flexibility. Building upon these identified vulnerabilities, the brief develops a policy framework distinguishing between cyclical execution failures and structural competitiveness decline. If current weaknesses reflect temporary manufacturing and technological setbacks, targeted interventions—particularly in advanced packaging research, HBM manufacturing capabilities, and foundry ecosystem development—may be sufficient. However, if markets are correctly pricing permanent losses in technological leadership, customer ecosystems, and manufacturing competitiveness, a broader industrial response is warranted. Recommended interventions include establishing government-supported advanced packaging research consortia modelled after international examples, strengthening semiconductor design ecosystems through process design kit and EDA toolchain development, expanding investment incentives for advanced semiconductor manufacturing, increasing specialised engineering talent through education and immigration policies, diversifying semiconductor production across allied jurisdictions to reduce geopolitical exposure, and improving corporate governance transparency to reduce Samsung's conglomerate valuation discount. A key methodological contribution of the paper is the proposal that reverse DCF analysis be institutionalised as a forward-looking industrial policy dashboard rather than viewed solely as an investment valuation technique. Unlike conventional indicators such as export volumes, R&D expenditure, or market share—which are inherently backward-looking—the reverse DCF aggregates market expectations regarding future technological competitiveness into a single market-implied profitability measure. The paper therefore develops a monitoring framework combining leading indicators, including HBM qualification progress, foundry customer acquisition, HBM4 development milestones, capital expenditure trends, and market-implied terminal margins, alongside lagging indicators such as export performance and profitability. Collectively, these metrics enable policymakers to assess whether industrial interventions are restoring confidence in South Korea's semiconductor competitiveness before deterioration becomes evident in macroeconomic statistics. The broader implication is that equity market expectations can serve as an early-warning system for national industrial policy wherever strategic sectors are dominated by nationally significant firms.

Artificial Intelligence in drug discovery and development: current landscape, challenges, and future perspectives Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming drug discovery and development, fields historically constrained by long timelines, high costs, and substantial attrition. Recent advances, particularly in generative modeling, enable an accelerated and increasingly systematic exploration of vast chemical and biological spaces, improving molecular interaction modeling and streamlining the identification and optimization of therapeutic candidates. However, the true utility of this expanded search space remains strictly bounded by the quality of upstream data and the logistical constraints of downstream experimental validation. Emerging platforms, including scaffold-aware and 3D molecular design tools (e.g., AlphaFold, MoleR, and PocketCrafter), single-cell foundation models, and large language models (LLMs), are expanding AI's applicability across the research and development pipeline, spanning target identification, drug discovery, lead optimization, phenotypic screening, and precision biology.AI is also increasingly integrated into preclinical and clinical research workflows, informing adaptive trial design, enabling AI-driven drug repurposing, and supporting the development of safer and more personalized therapies. While the U.S. FDA has approved numerous AI-enabled medical devices and software tools, no fully AI-discovered and AI-designed drug has yet received marketing approval. Nonetheless, several AI-originated candidates have progressed into clinical development, underscoring AI's growing translational impact. Collectively, these advances position AI as a collaborative "lab partner," capable of uncovering non-intuitive molecular designs, accelerating target and lead optimization, and enabling exploration of previously inaccessible chemical and biological space to inform downstream development and clinical decision-making. Despite gains in efficiency, scalability, and cost reduction, the broader impact of AI depends on access to high-quality multimodal data, robust regulatory and ethical frameworks, and careful recognition of methodological limitations. This review critically examines the evolution of AI approaches, highlighting key challenges and opportunities that shape the future of data-driven therapeutic innovation.

Visible and Near-Infrared Thin-Film Lithium Niobate Modulators with Thermo-Optic Bias High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Integrated photonics at submicrometer wavelengths holds the potential to enable scalable microsystems for quantum technologies, metrology, biophotonics, sensing, and displays, but on-chip modulation in this range remains challenging due to the limited availability of integration-ready materials that combine optical transparency with fast electro-optical (EO) modulation. Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) offers strong EO properties and a broad transparency window, and recent advances are rapidly expanding the functionality and performance of integrated TFLN platforms. At sub-μm wavelengths, however, the EO response is suppressed at low frequencies by rapid dielectric relaxation, hindering stable EO biasing and bias-sensitive operation. Here, we report sub-μm-wavelength TFLN Mach–Zehnder modulators (MZMs) that decouple bias control from radio frequency EO modulation by integrating thermo-optic (TO) phase shifters: the TO section provides stable bias tuning, while the EO section is reserved for high-frequency operation. Devices targeting wavelength bands from blue to 940 nm are fabricated in a single wafer-scale TFLN process, providing a foundry-compatible approach for bias-stable modulation across this spectral range. A blue-green MZM achieves an EO V π L of 0.91 V·cm at 488 nm, a TO P π of 40.4 mW at the same wavelength, and an EO bandwidth of >26.5 GHz at 461 nm, while a near-infrared MZM achieves an EO V π L of 2.81 V·cm, a TO P π of 150.3 mW, and an EO bandwidth of >26.5 GHz at 940 nm. We characterize the dielectric-relaxation time constants of the EO sections across all three designs and find values in the range of 0.9–6 μs. We further demonstrate bias stability exceeding 1 h at 461 nm and high-extinction-ratio pulse generation sustained for over 1.5 h at 875 nm, highlighting thermal biasing as a practical and scalable solution for bias-stable, high-speed TFLN modulators across the visible and submicrometer near-infrared spectrum.

Cross-Platform Neuromorphic Photodetectors: From Organic and Oxide to Perovskite, Wide-Bandgap, and Si-CMOS Conventional photodetectors and image sensors deliver high-fidelity digital outputs but face a growing data-movement bottleneck: the energy and latency cost of transferring raw pixel streams to off-chip memory and processors increasingly dominates over both sensing and computation in modern machine-vision pipelines. An emerging response is the neuromorphic photodetector, a class of optoelectronic device that converts incident light into an electrical signal while simultaneously storing, modulating, and pre-processing that signal in a manner inspired by biological synapses and retinas. Over the past decade, demonstrations have spanned at least eight material platforms—organic semiconductors, organic–carbon-nanotube hybrids, perovskite and perovskite hybrids, metal oxides (including ultra-wide-bandgap and printable variants), wide-bandgap III-nitrides and 4H-SiC, two-dimensional materials, photo-memristors, and silicon CMOS in-sensor compute architectures—and have been realised through four distinct architectural families: phototransistor synapses, photo-memristors, heterojunction in-sensor compute, and linear photovoltaic neural networks. Here, we provide a quantitative cross-platform benchmark across forty in-scope articles, identify persistent photoconductivity as a near-universal device-physical substrate underlying synaptic functionality, characterise the responsivity–speed–energy trade-off structure observed across platforms, and present a critical assessment of energy-reporting practice in the field. We further identify three best-practice exemplars from three independent material platforms that converge on operating biases of 0.01–0.1 V and energies of 0.07–0.8 fJ per event, and we propose a unified reporting framework to enable meaningful cross-platform benchmarking of next-generation neuromorphic photodetectors.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) Learning Applications Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are transforming learning environments by enabling personalized, adaptive, and intelligent educational systems. This research paper presents a systematic review of AI and ML applications in education, focusing particularly on their integration in e-learning platforms and adaptive learning technologies. The study synthesizes findings from recent scholarly literature, highlighting how AI/ML algorithms optimize learning paths, enhance student engagement, and improve academic performance across diverse educational contexts. It discusses challenges suchas ethical concerns, data privacy, and inequality in access to AI-powered learning tools. The uneven adoption of AI in education across global regions underscores the need for strategic policy and teacher training programs to ensure equitable technology integration. Additionally, the paper addresses applications beyond education, including AI/ML in cybersecurity, manufacturing, urban design, and intelligent systems, illuminating broader trends and future opportunities. This comprehensive analysis aims to provide an inclusive framework that informs educators, technologists, and policymakers about both the potentials and limitations of AI/ML in learning applications.

Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications The integration of multiomics technologies with artificial intelligence (AI) has become a transformative force in modern precision medicine, particularly within drug discovery. Multiomics approaches, including genome-wide association studies, transcriptomic profiling, proteomic interaction mapping, and metabolomic sequencing, provide unparalleled insights into the molecular dynamics of disease pathogenesis. Advanced AI methodologies, which leverage deep learning architectures, exhibit extraordinary capabilities in deciphering these intricate biological datasets, elucidating latent patterns, and constructing high-fidelity predictive models. The combined application of multiomics and AI has significant potential to accelerate target identification, streamline lead optimization processes, and enhance the precision of clinical trial designs. However, challenges persist, such as the need to harmonize disparate omics data streams, ensure reproducibility, and mitigate algorithmic biases. This review offers an in-depth analysis of multiomics applications across the drug development pipeline, covering target deconvolution, drug repositioning, and de novo compound discovery. It also explores the critical role of AI in drug discovery, focusing on virtual screening, pharmacokinetic modeling, and safety assessment frameworks. The fusion of multiomics with AI provides distinct advantages in hypothesis generation and data-driven discovery, opening new pathways for therapeutic innovation. By examining cases in oncology, neurodegenerative diseases, and cardiovascular conditions supported by robust technological infrastructures, this review presents a forward-thinking vision for future drug development. The convergence of these technologies not only enables comprehensive molecular understanding but also allows for more precise therapeutic interventions, marking the beginning of a new era in bench-to-clinic translational medicine.
